title: Rediscover the Z boson
audience: First-year university courses and International Masterclasses
summary: Select muon pairs, compute their invariant mass, find the resonance and measure its mass, the way the Z boson was confirmed in 1983 and is still calibrated at the LHC today.

reference.source: Particle Data Group, Review of Particle Physics

steps.title: Load collision events
steps.task: Load at least 1000 events. Use heplab.labs.practice_events() for the offline practice sample, or heplab.read(path) for CMS Open Data NanoAOD.
hints: Each event is a dictionary with an EventInfo record and a Muon list.

steps.title: Choose a muon selection
steps.task: Write an analysis configuration that keeps well-measured, isolated muons and pairs them with opposite electric charge.
hints: A Z boson is electrically neutral, so its two muons have opposite charge.
Muons from a Z decay carry tens of GeV of transverse momentum: try min_pt of 20 GeV.
Muons produced inside jets are surrounded by other particles. A relative isolation below 0.15 removes most of them.

steps.title: Compute one invariant mass by hand
steps.task: Take the first event that has two muons and compute the invariant mass of its first two muons yourself, from pt, eta, phi and mass.
hints: Build each four-vector: px = pt·cos φ, py = pt·sin φ, pz = pt·sinh η, E = √(px² + py² + pz² + m²).
Add the two four-vectors, then m = √(E² − |p|²).

steps.title: Histogram the dimuon mass
steps.task: Run the analysis with your selection over all events and look at the dimuon mass histogram. Where is the peak?
hints: heplab.notebook.show(result) draws it; drag across the plot to zoom into 60–120 GeV.

steps.title: Measure the Z mass
steps.task: Fit the peak and report the fitted mass and its uncertainty.
steps.answer: the result of heplab.fit_peak(result), or a (mass, uncertainty) pair in GeV
hints: The fit models the peak as a Gaussian on a flat background; mass is fit['values']['mean'].

steps.title: Explain the width
steps.task: Your fitted peak is wider than the Z boson's natural width of 2.5 GeV. Why?

choices.a: The Z boson lives longer in the detector than at rest.
choices.b: The detector measures muon momenta with finite resolution, which smears the peak.
choices.c: Opposite-charge muons always carry less energy.
choices.d: The fit used too few bins.

hints: The width you measure combines the particle's natural width and how precisely each muon is measured.
